objective: Core analysis framework: Audience, Purpose, Context (语篇语境) – three dimensions for analyzing non-fiction texts.；No universal audience exists; public writing targets interested or persuadable audiences; memos and maps often have mixed audiences.；Writing purposes are categorized into three types: to inform, to persuade, to analyze. learningGoals.statement: Identify the intended audience of a non-fiction text by analyzing its language, content, and format.
Determine whether a text serves a single or mixed purpose from the categories: inform, persuade, analyze.
Analyze context elements (legitimacy, time, professional circles, cultural background) that affect the meaning of a non-fiction text.

knowledgeNodes.name: 受众、目的、语境分析
knowledgeNodes.definition: The three core dimensions for analyzing non-fiction texts: audience (who the text is intended for), purpose (why the text is written: to inform, persuade, or analyze), and context (the situation surrounding the text including legitimacy, time, professional circles, cultural background).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Use knowledge of writing forms, and of the connections between form, audience, and purpose, to write summaries, information paragraphs, opinion pieces (i.e., series of paragraphs expressing an opinion), news reports, and personal reflections, incorporating graphic elements where necessary and appropriate.

questions.stem: A magazine article about electric cars uses technical terms like 'regenerative braking' and 'lithium-ion battery cycle life'. Which of the following is the most likely intended audience?

questions.stemIntent: Checks if student can infer audience from language and topic.
questions.commonMisconception: Student thinks all magazines target a 'general public' without considering specialized vocabulary.

options.label: A
options.text: The general public, because magazines are for everyone
options.feedbackWrong: Technical terms suggest the magazine is not written for a general audience; specific knowledge is assumed.

options.label: B
options.text: Mechanics and engineers, because the article uses automotive jargon

options.label: C

options.label: A

options.feedbackWrong: The text includes an argument (should be built), so it also aims to persuade, not just inform.

options.label: B
options.text: Only to persuade, because it argues for the highway
options.feedbackWrong: While it persuades, the inclusion of factual data shows it also informs; it serves both purposes.

options.label: C

options.label: D

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects an option implying a universal audience or fails to recognize that audience analysis is needed.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may mistakenly think there is a single universal audience for any text, ignoring the need to identify specific target readers.

miniLesson.explain: No text is written for everyone. Every non-fiction text targets a specific audience based on its purpose and context. A magazine article with technical terms like 'regenerative braking' and 'lithium-ion battery cycle life' is not meant for the general public but for readers with technical knowledge, such as mechanics or engineers. Identifying the audience helps you choose appropriate language, examples, and length in your own writing.
miniLesson.example: Consider an article about electric cars using terms like 'regenerative braking'. If you assume it's for everyone, you miss that the jargon points to an audience of engineers or enthusiasts. A children's book on the same topic would use simpler words and pictures, showing that audience determines content.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: No text is for everyone; ask 'Who needs to know this?'

guidedPractice.prompt: A website article titled 'How to Change Your Car’s Oil' uses step-by-step instructions with simple language and diagrams. Who is the most likely audience? Choose: (A) Professional mechanics, (B) Car owners who want to do it themselves, (C) Auto engineers, (D) The general public.
guidedPractice.answer: B. Car owners who want to do it themselves. The simple language and instructions target beginners, not professionals or the general public (who might not care).

guidedPractice.prompt: A memo from a company's CEO to all employees announces a new policy with terms like 'quarterly review' and 'performance metrics'. List two clues that help identify the audience as employees, and explain why a universal audience assumption would be wrong.
guidedPractice.answer: Clues: (1) Use of internal terms like 'quarterly review' implies shared context; (2) It is addressed 'to all employees'. Assuming a universal audience ignores that outsiders (customers) would not need this internal policy info. The language and format (memo) are specific to workplace communication.

guidedPractice.prompt: You find a blog post titled 'Why Electric Cars Are the Future' that uses persuasive language and mentions personal anecdotes. It includes links to scientific studies but also emotional appeals. Identify the intended audience, explain why it is not universal, and suggest how the text would differ if it were written for a different audience (e.g., policy makers vs. environmental activists).
guidedPractice.answer: Intended audience: environmentally conscious general readers interested in electric cars. It is not universal because it assumes interest in the topic and uses a mix of emotional and factual appeals. If written for policy makers, it would include more data on economic impact and regulation. For activists, it might emphasize grassroots actions. The language, evidence, and tone shift with audience.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects an option that assumes a text has only one purpose when it may have mixed purposes.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think every text serves only one purpose, ignoring that many texts combine informing, persuading, and analyzing.

miniLesson.explain: The lesson categorizes writing purposes into three types: to inform, to persuade, and to analyze. However, many non-fiction texts serve mixed purposes. For example, a newspaper editorial that argues for building a new highway (persuade) also provides data on construction costs and environmental impact (inform). Recognizing mixed purposes helps you understand the text more deeply and respond appropriately.
miniLesson.example: Consider an editorial: 'We must build the new highway to reduce traffic. Construction costs are estimated at $50 million and the environmental impact includes noise pollution.' This text both persuades (argues for action) and informs (provides facts).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Texts can wear two hats: inform and persuade at once. Always ask: 'What does this text want me to know? What does it want me to do?'

guidedPractice.prompt: A news article reports on a city council meeting, listing decisions made and votes. Identify the primary purpose(s): to inform, to persuade, or both?
An advertisement for a car includes fuel efficiency stats and a tagline 'Drive green, save money.' What purpose(s) does it serve?
guidedPractice.answer: both to inform and to persuade

guidedPractice.prompt: Write one sentence about a current issue that both informs and persuades. Then explain which parts inform and which persuade.
guidedPractice.answer: Example: 'Recycling reduces landfill waste by 30% (informs), so our community should adopt single-stream recycling (persuades).' Explanation: The statistic informs; the recommendation persuades.

reteachModules.trigger: I don't need to think about the culture or time; the text says what it means.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think context is just the topic or setting, ignoring deeper factors like cultural background, professional circles, and text legitimacy.

miniLesson.explain: Context analysis goes beyond the topic. It includes checking the text's legitimacy (is it from a credible source?), time required for the task (when was it written and for what deadline?), professional circles of the reader (what specialized knowledge do they have?), and cultural background (what values or assumptions shape the text?). These factors affect how the text should be interpreted and what inferences are valid.
miniLesson.example: A news report about a protest in a foreign country may use words like 'riot' or 'demonstration'. The cultural context (e.g., media freedom, government stance) influences which word is chosen and what bias exists. Ignoring this could lead to a misinterpretation of the event's severity.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think CULTURE: Credibility, Understanding, Legitimacy, Time, Professional circles, Every context matters.

guidedPractice.prompt: When analyzing a memo from a company's HR department, which context element is MOST important to check first?
guidedPractice.answer: Text legitimacy – ensure the memo is official and from a credible source within the company.

guidedPractice.prompt: A scientific article from 1980 uses the term 'global warming' while a 2020 article uses 'climate crisis'. What context element explains this difference?
guidedPractice.answer: Time/era – the cultural and scientific understanding of climate change evolved, affecting terminology and urgency.

guidedPractice.prompt: A marketing report for a luxury car brand uses formal language and mentions 'engineering precision' and 'heritage'. Besides the product, what professional circles and cultural background likely influence the text's tone and content?
guidedPractice.answer: Professional circles: automotive engineers and luxury market analysts. Cultural background: emphasis on tradition and quality in high-end markets (e.g., German or British luxury car culture).

questions.stem: A magazine article about electric cars uses technical terms like 'regenerative braking' and 'lithium-ion battery cycle life'. Which statement best describes its audience?
options: It is written for the general public because anyone can read magazines.
It is written for a specific audience, such as engineers or car enthusiasts, who understand the technical terms.
It is written for a universal audience because the topic is electric cars.
The audience cannot be determined from the language used.

questions.stem: Read the following text: 'The teacher reminded students to submit their assignments by Friday or they would lose marks.' Identify the intended audience and explain why it is not a universal audience. Provide one clue from the text that supports your answer.
questions.rubric: Student must: (1) identify audience as students (1 point), (2) state that it is not universal because it refers to specific school-related context (1 point), (3) provide a clue from the text such as 'teacher', 'students', 'assignments', or 'lose marks' (1 point). Accept equivalent phrasing. 3 points total.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select the correct answer in the multiple-choice question and score at least 2 out of 3 on the open-ended question rubric.

questions.stem: A government report on climate change includes scientific data and then recommends actions citizens should take. Which of the following best describes the author's purpose(s)?
options: To inform only
To persuade only
Both to inform and to persuade
To analyze only

questions.stem: Read the following short text: 'Our school's recycling program reduced waste by 20% last year. We urge all students to participate so we can reach 30% this year.' Identify the purpose(s) of this text. Then explain which parts serve each purpose.
questions.rubric: Student correctly identifies both inform and persuade as purposes. They explain that the first sentence (statistic) informs, and the second sentence (urge) persuades. Partial credit if one purpose is correctly identified with supporting evidence.

retestCards.passRule: Student correctly identifies mixed purposes in at least two different types of texts, demonstrating understanding that many non-fiction texts serve more than one purpose.

questions.stem: When analyzing a text, which of the following is NOT an element of context according to the Audience-Purpose-Context framework?
options: Text legitimacy (credibility of source)
Time required for the task
The author's favorite color
Professional circles of the reader

questions.stem: A blog post from 2015 discusses 'the dangers of social media' and uses phrases like 'addictive by design'. Another blog post from 2024 on the same topic argues that social media can be 'a tool for community building'. What context element(s) likely explain the difference in tone and argument? Explain in 2-3 sentences.
questions.rubric: Identifies time/era as a key context element (cultural shift in understanding social media). Also acceptable: changes in cultural background or professional circles (e.g., researchers vs. activists). Must mention context and how it influences the text.
